claims.text: The onset and progression of the phase transition in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are primarily governed by size-dependent melting-point depression caused by the Gibbs–Thomson effect.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are initially solid.
The starting nanoparticles are compositionally homogeneous.
The starting sample is polydisperse and contains a broad range of nanoparticle sizes.
Size-sorted populations near 5 nm, 20 nm, and 50 nm can provide a controlled comparison while composition is held constant.
Smaller nanoparticles have greater curvature and an elevated surface-to-volume ratio.
The Gibbs–Thomson effect lowers the effective melting temperature of smaller nanoparticles.
High nanoparticle curvature increases the energetic contribution of the surface.
The curvature-associated surface energy causes surface premelting to begin earlier in smaller nanoparticles.
Premelting progressively propagates inward from the nanoparticle surface.
Smaller-diameter nanoparticles will exhibit an earlier onset of premelting than larger nanoparticles.
Smaller-diameter nanoparticles will exhibit a broader melting transition than larger nanoparticles.
Melting-onset temperature will decrease monotonically as particle size decreases.
Polydisperse nanoparticle samples typically show overlapping melting-transition signatures.
The size-dependent effect is expected to be significant mainly below a critical diameter of approximately 50 nm.
Above approximately 50 nm, the transition may approach bulk-like behavior.
The nanoparticle size effect on melting is well documented.
Compositional or structural variations during heating may alter the magnitude of melting-point depression.
A lack of a statistically significant systematic relationship between size and phase-transition onset or progression would falsify the proposed size-governed mechanism.
